title: Dzinglski v. Weirton Steel Corporation
lead: An investigation left a manager without his job, but the West Virginia court distinguished the distress of being discharged from an outrageous way of discharging him.

actors.name: Weirton Steel Corporation
actors.role: Employee-owned employer that investigated and discharged him

actors.name: Justice Neely
actors.role: Author of the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals opinion

proceedings: Trial court directed verdicts on other theories but submitted intentional infliction of emotional distress; jury awarded compensatory and punitive damages.
Trial court struck punitive damages; Supreme Court of Appeals reversed the remaining judgment.
limits: The accusations were not findings of criminal conduct. The opinion ends “Reversed,” without expressly directing a new trial or dismissal with prejudice.
The court addressed amendment, limitations, and punitive damages after saying those questions were unnecessary to reversal.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Employee ownership brings an accusation
paragraphs: Andrew Dzinglski had worked for National Steel for twenty-five years when its Weirton operation became employee-owned in January 1984. Workers accepted substantial cuts in pay and benefits for stock. During the negotiations, their union proposed removing managers considered detrimental to the new company and eliminating outside contractors when employees could do the work more cheaply. Valley Systems, an industrial cleaner with which Dzinglski dealt daily as a general foreman, lost its contract.

Security supervisor Richard McKittrick then received anonymous accusations that Dzinglski had accepted kickbacks from Valley. The caller eventually identified himself as Tim Lawson, a foreman who had worked under Dzinglski. Lawson alleged payments for salaried supervisors who did no work, gifts, meals and travel, and use of Weirton supplies. He identified former Valley employees William Baxter and Charles Fraizer as corroborating witnesses. Vice president William Doepken ordered an investigation. Confronted in late May, Dzinglski denied wrongdoing; the company suspended him with pay under its management-investigation policy.

sections.title: The evidence remains mixed, but the job ends
sections.cue: Follow the investigation without treating allegations as findings.
paragraphs: An internal audit examined records, while McKittrick interviewed witnesses. He said his memoranda reached only four company officials. Baxter described deliveries of bacon, a bathroom vanity, bolt cutters and a camera, altered invoices, meals and a motel room. Some items had possible work purposes: bolt cutters, for example, could open former employees’ lockers. Fraizer described the camera, supplies and lunches. Valley owner Eugene Valentine acknowledged gifts as business goodwill, but said the camera was for work and the vanity for Valley’s trailer office.

Doepken reviewed the accusations with Dzinglski again in July; he again denied wrongdoing. Witnesses corroborated some accusations and the audit found billing irregularities, but Lawson’s charges were never fully substantiated, and there was no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by Dzinglski. Weirton nevertheless believed the accusations impaired his effectiveness as a labor manager and honorably discharged him on October 31, 1984.

sections.title: One claim reaches the jury
sections.cue: Explain how the case narrowed at trial.
paragraphs: Dzinglski sued in October 1985. His amended complaint in October 1987 asserted wrongful discharge, promissory estoppel, breach of good faith and fair dealing, defamation, negligent investigation, violation of public policy, and punitive damages. At the May 13, 1992 pretrial conference, two weeks before trial, he added intentional infliction of emotional distress, also called outrage.

The trial judge directed verdicts for Weirton on wrongful discharge, estoppel and good faith because Dzinglski was employed at will and the discharge violated no public policy. Defamation and negligent investigation failed because the investigation and limited internal communications were qualifiedly privileged; defamation was also time-barred. The jury nevertheless awarded $500,000 compensatory and $150,000 punitive damages on outrage. The judge later struck the punitive award. Weirton appealed the submission of outrage, the late amendment and timeliness; Dzinglski sought restoration of punitive damages.

sections.title: The court separates termination from abusive treatment
sections.cue: Connect the governing distinction to this investigation.
paragraphs: Justice Neely, writing for the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, explained that outrage requires intentional or reckless causation of severe distress by conduct exceeding acceptable bounds of decency. Abuse of authority can contribute to that showing, but insisting on legal rights in a permissible manner does not become outrageous merely because distress is foreseeable. A lawful discharge therefore does not automatically defeat a claim concerning an abusive manner of discharge.

Earlier decisions marked the distinction. Farmer allowed separate discriminatory and outrageous conduct to support distinct claims; Magnuson and Viestenz involved distress attributable to discharge itself. West Virginia’s Harless likewise allowed an independent outrage claim only when its separate elements existed. Embarrassment and financial loss from losing a job could not simply be relabeled an independent tort.

Here, Weirton had a right and obligation to investigate reported managerial improprieties. Records review, interviews, paid suspension, restricted memoranda, and private opportunities to answer the charges were appropriate. The court considered the manner of discharge far from outrageous and the company’s motivations proper. It acknowledged Dzinglski’s distress but attributed it to losing his job. Failure fully to substantiate the charges did not convert the investigation into outrage.

Qualified privilege supplied additional support. It protected good-faith communications about a legitimate interest or duty to persons sharing that interest. Bad motive or excessive publication could defeat it, but neither had been shown here. This was protection for this investigation’s actual scope and circumstances, not unconditional immunity for employers.

sections.title: Reversal, with additional answers for future cases
sections.cue: Keep the necessary holding separate from the additional rulings.
paragraphs: On May 26, 1994, the court reversed the $500,000 judgment for insufficient outrageous conduct. Although that disposed of the appeal, it addressed the remaining questions to clarify the law for the bar.

The late amendment was permissible under Rule 15 because the distress theory concerned the investigation already in dispute, caused no unfair prejudice, and could be met by Weirton, which had not requested a discovery continuance. It also related back: it added a theory about the same conduct, rather than different underlying facts, and was therefore timely.

The court also agreed with striking the additional $150,000 punitive award. The jury had characterized Weirton’s conduct as wanton, oppressive and reckless, but the court explained that a distress award without physical trauma, based on intentionally outrageous conduct, could itself serve punitive and deterrent purposes. Adding punishment for the same acts would duplicate recovery here. That discussion did not revive the compensatory award, which independently failed. The reported disposition was simply reversal, and no separate opinion appears.
